a.text: An open grave. The earth around it is torn — but not by a spade. It was pushed apart from below.

b.text: The hole is exactly your size. There is still a hollow in the soil where your head rested.

c.text: You remember nothing before the cold. Not even a name.

again.text: Your grave. It feels strange to call it that. It feels stranger that it fits.

a.text: The headstone is older than the others, smooth with four hundred years of rain.

b.text: No name. No dates. Only a single candle carved into the stone — unlit.

a.speaker: Tilde
a.text: You were *in* there. I dug around that stone for three summers. Nobody's name on it. Nobody's ever visited it.

b.speaker: Tilde
b.text: …Are you a ghost? You don't look see-through. Just sort of… grey.

choices.text: I don't know what I am.

c1.speaker: Tilde
c1.text: Well, that makes two of us. I'm Tilde. I dig the graves. Usually people stay in them.

c2.speaker: Tilde
c2.text: Saint Ebba's. The graveyard above Candlewick, in Hollowmere Vale. You're standing in the bit for people nobody remembers.

c3.speaker: Tilde
c3.text: Right. A quiet ghost. That's the worst kind.

d.speaker: Tilde
d.text: Go down to the village. Ask for Mother Odile at the candle shrine. And — try to be memorable. Folk here forget things.

again.speaker: Tilde
again.text: Still here? Candlewick's down the road, past the signpost. Mind the lake. Sometimes it glows.

a.text: A weathered signpost. Three arms, the paint long gone. Someone has scratched new words into the wood:

b.text: EAST — Candlewick.   NORTH — Saint Ebba's.   SOUTH-WEST — the Mere Ferry.   A fourth arm has been sawn off. Only a nail remains.

a.text: Hollowmere lies still and black. Far below the surface, something glows — a small, warm light, like a lantern held by a patient hand.

b.text: You watch it for a long time. Then it dims, and for a moment you feel as if someone has said goodbye.

a.text: A shrine of name-candles. Each stub has a name scratched into the wax — Bertil, Gisla, Ludo, Tilde…

b.text: Eight of them burn. The ninth has never been lit.

c.text: None of them carries your name.

a.text: The village well. A bucket on a fraying rope. Someone has tied a ribbon to the crank — the kind you tie so you won't forget something.
A small bell tower. The bell hangs silent; its rope has been cut clean through.

b.text: Carved into a post, almost hidden: "By order of the Silent Nine."

a.text: The Old Silver Mine. Cold air breathes out of the dark. Somewhere deep inside, someone is counting — slowly, over and over.

b.text: "…four… five…" The voice never reaches six. (The mine opens in the next phase of development.)

a.text: An old timber bridge. Someone has carved small notches into the railing — one for every crossing, it seems. Thousands of them.
The windmill turns, though there is hardly any wind. Flour dust glitters on the door. Inside, someone is humming a tune you almost recognise.
A ring of standing stones on the hilltop. Nine places, cut flat into the rock. Only eight stones.

b.text: Where the ninth should stand there is only moss, and the moss grows in the shape of a stone that was never raised.

again.text: Eight stones. One empty place. The wind sounds different when it passes through the gap.

a.text: The stump of a watch tower, broken like a tooth. Soot on the inner walls — a fire burned here, long ago, for a long time.

b.text: Scratched into a stone near the doorway: "WE WATCHED. NOTHING CAME. WE WATCHED ANYWAY."

a.text: A small camp at the edge of the woods. The fire is still warm, the tent empty. Whoever sleeps here left a cup of tea that is not yet cold.

b.text: You sit for a while and listen to the fire. For a moment, nothing in the world is forgetting anything.

a.speaker: Mother Odile
a.text: Tilde told me about you. Came out of Saint Ebba's own unmarked stone, she says. And here you stand — and I'll forget your face the moment you turn around.

b.speaker: Mother Odile
b.text: Unless… sit with me. A candle needs a name, love. Wax forgets everything else.

c.speaker: Mother Odile
c.text: So. What shall the world call you, now that it's ready to listen?

d.speaker: Mother Odile
d.text: {name}. There — scratched into the wax. Now you're *someone*. Try not to waste it.

e.speaker: Mother Odile
e.text: Old Ansel down in the silver mine still counts his lost men every night. Somebody ought to make him stop. Maybe somebody nobody remembers.

again.speaker: Mother Odile
again.text: Your candle burns nicely, {name}. The mine is east of the lake. And if you hear bells in the hills — those towers have been silent for a hundred years.

a.text: A bell tower nobody has climbed in a hundred years. The rope is rotten, but it might hold.

rung.text: The bell's voice rolls out over the Whisperwood. For a heartbeat the trees and stones seem to remember their own shapes more clearly. Far away, very faintly, another bell answers.

done.text: The bell still hums. This land remembers you now.

a.speaker: A Faded Woman
a.text: …was there a door here? I had a door. Blue, I think. Or was that a name…

b.speaker: A Faded Woman
b.text: Name? I'll know it when I hear it. Will you say it to me, if you ever find it?

c.text: She keeps turning in a slow circle, looking for a door that isn't there.

a.speaker: A Faded Man
a.text: Counting. I was counting something. Sheep? Days? …Steps home. How many steps is home?
A signpost, the letters almost gone: A_DERS_Y. Nobody in Candlewick knows this village. It is on no map.

b.text: Everything here is grey as ash, and so quiet you can hear your own heartbeat. This is the Hush — the place where the world forgets itself.

a.text: Nobody answers. Through the round window you see a table laid for two, and a candle burned down to nothing — but the wax is still warm.
